We answer the four questions of \S\ref{sec:bg-rq}: RQ1 information
(\S\ref{sec:eval-info}), RQ2 effect inside the kernel (\S\ref{sec:eval-kernel}), RQ3
cost (\S\ref{sec:eval-cost}) and RQ4 robustness (\S\ref{sec:eval-robust}), then the
ablations (\S\ref{sec:eval-ablate}) and where the learned policy does not help
(\S\ref{sec:eval-loss}).

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Setup}
\label{sec:eval-setup}

\finding{Platform.} \xv on QEMU \todo{version}, one hart. A kernel run repeats exactly:
the same program, stream, memory size and policy give the same faults every time, so the
uncertainty we report comes from which streams were run, not from run-to-run noise.

\finding{Workloads.} Fourteen (Table~\ref{tab:workloads}). The learned models are trained
on six of them (B-tree, graph, key-value, LZW, matmul, sort) and run unchanged on the
other eight, which include replays of Twitter cache traces~\citep{yang2020twitter}, an
eleven-pattern synthetic suite with known answers, and application-shaped programs. Every
program's reference string is checked, reference by reference, against an independent
model of the program.

\finding{Memory and runs.} The resident limit is 5, 10 or 20\% of each program's pages:
74 streams at 10\%, 51 at 5\% and 20\% (one per variant); the pattern and application
programs run their first 50,000 accesses. 2,375 kernel runs in total.
% src: week_16 report section "What was run"; AUSTRA_HANDOFF START HERE section 6

\finding{Policies.} In the kernel: FIFO, \clock, Aging, LFU; ARC~\citep{megiddo2003arc},
LHD~\citep{beckmann2018lhd} and S3-FIFO~\citep{yang2023s3fifo} in the form a kernel can
run (\S\ref{sec:impl}); the learned linear score with one global set of weights (and
per-workload weights where stated); and five heavier models, trained on the same six
workloads and run on ten streams at every memory size. \belady is offline and appears
only in simulation. \todo{closest learned prior work re-run on our traces, e.g.\
LeCaR~\citep{vietri2018lecar} or CACHEUS~\citep{rodriguez2021cacheus} with
kernel-visible inputs; or one sentence on why it is excluded}

\finding{Metrics.} Faults are zero-fill plus swap faults, relative to \clock on the same
stream and memory. We average with a geometric mean over the streams of each workload,
then over the 14 workloads with equal weight, so a workload with 17 streams counts once.
95\% intervals resample the workloads, then the streams inside them. Decision cost is in
instructions, counted exactly (\S\ref{sec:impl}), with 68 candidates per eviction.
\todo{page writes for the current build (the week-14 build, per-workload weights at 10\%,
cut writes by up to 96.5\%; not yet reported for the final runs)}

\subsection{RQ1: Does the Kernel See Enough?}
\label{sec:eval-info}
% Simulator results (the kernel cannot run oracle-input models). Filled-memory start.

\finding{With kernel signals only, more capacity does not help.} Boosted trees over the
same kernel-visible signals tie the linear score where both work (btree test 0.834 vs.\
0.835) and lose where data are scarce (LZW held-out 1.068 vs.\ 0.813; matmul held-out
0.803 vs.\ 0.671) (Table~\ref{tab:info}).

\finding{Oracle inputs help only on familiar workloads.} Given information a kernel never
has (exact recency, frequency, reuse history), the best trees and networks are 2--5\%
better than the best linear score on the workloads they were trained on. On real Redis
and SQLite traces, recorded on Linux, every richer model is 22--41\% worse than the
linear one, and a linear score with oracle inputs reaches $3\times$ \clock on Redis.
What the kernel cannot see is not what limits a learned policy here; what it can see
transfers better.
% src: week-15 report "What the wider comparison says" and "Transfer to unseen workloads";
% week_16 tables/model_comparison.tex and tables/transfer.tex (redis-real linear F+K 3.000)

\finding{\feat{idle} carries the policy.} Adding \feat{idle} (scans since the page was
last found accessed) to a feature subset that lacks it cuts faults by a median of 71\% on
graph, 29\% on btree and 20\% on kv (Appendix, Figure~\ref{fig:marginal}). This is the signal MGLRU
generations and DAMON ages already track.

\label{sec:eval-kernel}

\label{tab:kernel}

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{The comparisons that matter, with 95\% intervals (resampling workloads, then

\label{tab:ci}

\finding{The linear score beats \clock at 10\% memory} (0.914, interval 0.85--0.98;
Table~\ref{tab:ci}). At 5\% (0.979) and 20\% (0.887) it is better on average, but the
intervals include 1: a few workloads decide the average.

\finding{It is level with ARC, not better.} ARC, in kernel form, beats \clock at 5\% and
10\% (0.946 and 0.943, intervals below 1) and is level at 20\% (0.986). The linear score
against ARC is 1.035, 0.970 and 0.899 at 5, 10 and 20\% memory; no interval excludes 1,
and the gap moves in the learned score's favour as memory grows. LHD is the most uneven
(0.63 on graph at 10\%, level elsewhere); S3-FIFO in kernel form is not better than
\clock at any size; FIFO, Aging and LFU are worse than \clock everywhere, by 4--34\%.

\finding{Where it wins.} The learned score does best where recency is a poor guide:
btree and kv (0.82--0.96 at every size), the heap programs (0.73 at 10\%, 0.56 at 20\%),
pointer chasing, and the hash join at 20\% (0.55) (Table~\ref{tab:kernel}).

\finding{The simulator predicts the kernel.} For the kernel forms of ARC, S3-FIFO and LHD,
kernel faults divided by simulator faults are 0.995, 1.014 and 0.984 (geometric mean
over 74 streams; median stream within 1.5\%), as for FIFO, Aging, LFU and the linear
score earlier (within about 4\%), once the simulator starts from filled memory.

\subsection{RQ3: What Does a Decision Cost, and When Does It Pay?}
\label{sec:eval-cost}

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Instructions the kernel spends choosing one victim among 68 candidates, counted
exactly (QEMU instruction-counting mode, repeatable to 0.3\%), and as a multiple of the
linear score.}
\label{tab:cost}
\vskip 0.1in
\begin{center}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{\wsixteen/cost}}
\end{center}
\vskip -0.1in
\end{table}

\finding{Whole numbers lose nothing.} With 8 fractional bits for the weights, every
selected linear model is within $\pm0.002$ of its floating-point fault ratio.
% src: ML_REPORT 8, quant table (pre-refit models; the method is unchanged)

\finding{The learned score has the highest overhead of any policy that pays.} Choosing a victim
costs 22,803 instructions with 68 candidates, about 340 per candidate: 55$\times$ \clock,
about twice ARC (11,934) and LHD (14,199) (Table~\ref{tab:cost}). The rest of an
eviction (finding the candidates and bookkeeping) costs about 6,000--6,500 instructions
for every policy. The heavier models cost 20$\times$ (boosted and ranking trees) to
150$\times$ (deeper MLP) the linear score. Sampling 32 candidates holds the linear score
at about 11,700 instructions whatever the memory size, for 0 to 1 point of faults.
% src: tables/cost.tex; week-15 report section "What choosing a victim costs, and when it pays"

\finding{Whether a saved fault pays depends on the device.} Assuming one instruction per
nanosecond and a fault cost we did not measure, the linear score of each workload pays
for itself on a hard disk (8\,ms per fault) on every workload where it saves faults (time
0.58--0.94 of \clock's) and roughly breaks even on fast flash (100\,\textmu s): 0.90 of
\clock's time on graph, 1.51 on btree, where 230 candidates make the scan expensive.
With 16 sampled candidates it beats \clock in total time even on flash for LZW (0.91)
and the Twitter replays (0.93). The CNN and MLP never pay: their break-even fault cost is
10--670\,ms.

\subsection{RQ4: Robustness and Generalisation}
\label{sec:eval-robust}

\finding{Workloads never seen in training.} Eight of the 14 workloads were never in
training. At 10\% memory the global score is 0.73 on heap churn, 0.85 on the Twitter
replays, 0.86 on pointer chasing and 0.87 on the pattern suite, level on the hash join,
Bloom filter and application programs, and 1.12 on SpMV (Table~\ref{tab:kernel}).
% src: kmain_A_01 (linear, global row)

\finding{Controls behave.} On the uniform pattern every online policy is within 0.0003 of
the analytical miss rate and no model gains, so nothing leaks from training; on the loop
pattern MRU matches \belady and the recency policies miss every time.
% src: week-15 report "Transfer to unseen workloads" (simulator)

\finding{Failures are specific and repeat.} Matrix multiply at 5\% (1.72, with only two
frames), SpMV at 5\% and 10\% (1.10, 1.12), and graph with the global weights at 5\% and
20\% (1.01, 1.60; graph's own weights give 0.60 at 10\%). A guard that falls back to
\clock (\S\ref{sec:design-wrong}) cuts the worst case from 1.86 to 1.36 in simulation, but
the kernel runs have none.
% src: AUSTRA_HANDOFF START HERE section 0; kmain_A_005/01/02

\finding{Selection and data noise are small.} Refitting the linear score on three datasets
drawn with different sampling seeds moves its result by at most 0.0005 (kernel signals),
under 0.3\%, against the 1--14\% differences between policies.
% src: week-15 report "Noise floor"

\subsection{Ablations}
\label{sec:eval-ablate}

\finding{Model capacity (A2), in the kernel.} Trained on the same six workloads, the CNN
and deeper MLP are level with the linear score at every size (CNN 0.981, 1.003, 1.028 of
the linear score's faults at 5, 10, 20\%; MLP 1.006, 1.000, 1.039), at 87$\times$ and
150$\times$ its cost. Ranking trees lose to \clock at 5\% and 10\% (1.09, 1.40; 32$\times$
\clock on one SpMV stream). Set-attention is the least stable: its result changes by a
median of 2$\times$ (up to 14$\times$) with what is in memory at the start.
% src: ci_main.tex; week_16 report section "The models trained on all workloads"; week-15 "Why the kernel and the simulator disagree"

\finding{Training scope.} Trained on one workload instead of all six, four of the five
heavier kinds are worse (simulator; set-attention 1.48 vs.\ 0.90 of \clock).
% src: tables/trainedall.tex

\finding{Training data and probation (A3).} With uniform candidate sampling, graph's models
were $\geq1.25\times$ \clock; recency-stratified recording and probation brought three of
four fixed feature groups to 0.66--0.81 on graph validation and removed every catastrophic
subset on sort and matmul. Probation is decisive on graph (0.810 $\rightarrow$ 0.613 from
0 to 4 scans) and harmful on matmul, where 5 frames leave little choice. One round of
DAgger did not help.
% src: ML_REPORT 7.2-7.3 (pre-refit; the effect sizes, not the exact values, carry over).
% \todo{rerun the v1/v2 and probation ablations on the current datasets, or say "first version"}

\finding{Sensitivity to the sample size (A5).} 32 candidates cost 0--1 point of faults, 16 cost 1--2 points
(LZW 0.837 $\rightarrow$ 0.842 $\rightarrow$ 0.858; Twitter replays 0.876 $\rightarrow$
0.875 $\rightarrow$ 0.884).
% src: week-15 report "In the xv6 kernel"

\subsection{Where the Learned Policy Does Not Help}
\label{sec:eval-loss}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Tiny memory:} matrix multiply at 5\% (two frames) is 1.72 of \clock.
\item \textbf{Indirect access:} SpMV at 5\% and 10\% (1.10, 1.12).
\item \textbf{One set of weights for every program:} graph at 5\% and 20\% (1.01, 1.60),
  though graph's own weights reach 0.60 at 10\%. Choosing weights per program
  automatically is open.
\item \textbf{Nothing to learn:} Bloom filter (every policy 1.00) and the application
  programs at 5\%.
\item \textbf{No write marks:} on the real Redis trace the kernel-signal score is 1.11 of
  \clock in simulation, where the dirty bit carries no signal; LRU is the best simple
  policy there (0.93).
\item \textbf{Fast storage:} on flash the btree score costs more time than it saves.
\end{itemize}
